projectOutComesReport:
Overview

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers have made efforts to develop realistic simulation models that predict the number of COVID-19 deaths and evaluate the effectiveness of policy interventions. However, these models are developed based on a variety of approaches and thus produce radically different predictions, creating confusion among policymakers and the public about the severity of the situation and how best to respond.

Therefore, our key objectives included: (1) the implementation of a novel ensemble modeling approach that can be used to combine predictions from multiple models into a consensus, (2) the design and development of an interactive web-based dashboard to serve as an open and accessible tool for users to compare between models, (3) the provision of mentorship and research opportunities for students at a range of academic levels and (4) engagement with the broader public, the modeling community, and policymakers.

(1)  Ensemble Modeling Approach

One objective of this project was to combine predictions from a variety of models that simulate the spread of COVID-19. This is a challenging endeavor because the temporal resolution of the forecasts (i.e. the predicted number of COVID-19 deaths over time) is inconsistent from model to model. The project results reveal that an approach referred to as data imputation can be used to fill in the gaps in model predictions to overcome this challenge. Specifically, for every model, given a from-date and to-date, imputation allows us to estimate how many deaths that the model would predict, even if the raw model data is not explicitly available. In essence, we have devised methods to ?predict the predictions?. Leveraging this model of imputation, we investigated ways to use machine learning approaches to combine predictions into a consensus that minimizes the deviation from the (later) observed ground truth. However, our investigated models are outperformed by state-of-the-art ensemble modeling. This is still ongoing and promising work with many potential interesting research directions.

(2)  Interactive Dashboard

We have developed and made available an open and accessible web-based dashboard (https://covid-ensemble.gmu.edu) called the COVID-19 Ensemble Dashboard that allows users to compare between predictions generated by a wide range of models as well as visualize the degree of uncertainty/confidence levels associated with those predictions. The COVID-19 Ensemble Dashboard will both improve knowledge discovery and support decision-making during infectious disease outbreaks.

(3)  Student Mentorship and Research Training

Our team made it a priority to provide research experience and mentoring for a range of students at all levels of academia. Apart from the PIs, our research team has consisted of a postdoctoral researcher, five graduate student researchers, eight undergraduate researchers, and nine high school research interns. These students were mentored as a part of the Aspiring Scientists Summer Internship Program and the Provost?s Summer Team Impact Projects at George Mason University over two summers (2020-21). Students received training to build skills including scientific writing, engagement with the professional scientific community, and the communication of research and results. The mentorship and training they received over the summer had the potential to shape their futures as they go on to make decisions about post-secondary education in STEM and their careers. This project yielded a total of five journal or conference papers and fifteen oral or poster presentations led by student researchers. At this time, of the five papers, three are published and two are under review. An additional publication, led by the postdoctoral researcher, is in writing.

(4)  Engagement with Broader Public, Modeling Community, and Decision Makers 

COVID-19 response requires interdisciplinary collaboration and strong ties with stakeholders in public health. The project PIs have worked to develop multi-institutional synergies and collaborations with experts in epidemiology, social behavioral and economic sciences, and computer sciences. Examples of synergistic activities include the organization of interdisciplinary workshops, seminars, and conferences (namely the 1st ACM SIGSPATIAL International Workshop on Modeling and Understanding the Spread of COVID-19 and the 2nd ACM SIGSPATIAL International Workshop on Spatial Computing for Epidemiology) and the and editorial roles in a journal special issues such as ACM Transactions on Spatial Algorithms and Systems Special Issues on Special Issue on Understanding the Spread of COVID-19 that call for interdisciplinary collaboration towards pandemic preparedness and response. Additionally, we have connected with various stakeholders in public health such as Fairfax County, the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO), and the National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO) with the aim to shift research into practice and foster new research directions.

(5)  Other Outcomes

Other achievements include methodological advancements including improving simulation models of COVID-19 spread and leveraging novel spatiotemporal datasets to understand the spread of COVID-19 better.

abstractText:
Secure multi-party computation (MPC) allows multiple distrusting parties to perform joint computations on their data without exposing the data to one another. Due to their promising security guarantees, the cryptographic protocols for MPC have gained unprecedented exposure in the last decade. With the proliferation of large, distributed systems and computations such as Tor and blockchain, there is an urgent need for large-scale MPC to ensure security and privacy for these applications. However, large-scale applications pose some unique challenges for the design of MPC protocols. There are thousands of parties, often with unequal resources, and a small number of parties are likely to fail during a protocol execution. This project proposes to design MPC protocols to address these challenges. The project’s novelties are the design of new MPC protocols satisfying the requirements of large-scale distributed applications. 

Specifically, the investigators put forward a new framework for committee-based MPC for large-scale secure computations. These protocols distribute the computations across thousands of parallel committees to maximize the utilization of available resources for improved throughput. The designed protocols optimally choose committees and committee sub-protocols that optimize resource utilization and security. Additionally, they handle party failure and provide efficient oblivious access and search capabilities over data generated in these computations.  The team of researchers combines techniques from prior work on secure computation (MPC) and oblivious data structures to simultaneously achieve all of these goals. The project’s impacts are to enable new classes of privacy-preserving computation, analytics, and applications geared to the needs of real-world distributed systems.

program: SaTC: Secure and Trustworthy Cyberspace, MEDIUM PROJECT, RES IN UNDERGRAD INST-RESEARCH
projectOutComesReport:
Secure computation protocols allow two or more parties, each holding private data, to collaborate and perform some agreed upon computation, revealing nothing about the input beyond what is learned from the result.  An example might be two entities, each holding user data, agreeing to train a model on their datasets without either having to provide their data to the other party.  

Over the last fifty years, secure computation protocols have evolved to handle larger dataset sizes and increasingly complex computational goals. More recently, with the rise of mobile computing devices, and with the introduction of blockchain networks, there is also a need for protocols that can support larger numbers of participating parties. While early applications envisioned a handful of parties computing on their own data, in today’s computing environments, one can imagine a large distributed network of participants computing on other people’s data while maintaining its privacy.  

This research effort has explored mechanisms for scaling secure computation to support thousands or tens of thousands of participants. It resulted in several foundational results that improved the communication costs in state-of-the-art protocols by up to three or four orders of magnitude when computing in networks involving thousands of parties. It also led to results improving on the best protocols for particular computations of interest, such as multiparty private set intersection, in which a large number of participants find the input items common to the whole group.  Finally, although the work is still in progress, this project led to new meaningful security definitions and protocols for ensuring that large scale computations of this nature are resilient, providing output even when parties might abandon the protocol partway through.   

The project has supported multiple PhD students as they pursued their degrees, including one that completed his dissertation entirely on the subject of large scale secure computation.  The results have been published in top venues for computer science research and were presented by those PhD students. The project facilitated a strong collaboration with other Universities in the Washington D.C. area, including with co-PIs at George Washington University and the U.S. Naval academy, as well as with the University of Maryland.  Additionally, it supported new course development in the areas of cryptography and secure computation.

abstractText:
Social media data can provide important clues and local knowledge that can help emergency managers and responders better comprehend and capture the evolving nature of many disasters. Yet humans alone cannot grasp the vast data generated by social media, so computers are used to assist.  Very little is currently known about how to leverage the skills of humans and machines when they work together (human-machine teaming) to identify meaningful patterns in social media data.  Therefore, the fundamental issues this Rapid Response Research (RAPID) project seeks to address are 1) understanding the process of real-time decisions that human digital volunteers make when they rapidly convert social media data into structured codes the machine (Artificial Intelligence algorithms) can understand, and 2) using this knowledge to improve human-machine teaming.  This project advances the field by revealing the unique abilities that both humans and machines bring when working together to comprehend social media patterns during an evolving disaster.  It supports education and diversity by providing research experiences to diverse students, as well as generating data useful for interdisciplinary courses teaching teamwork, social media analysis, and human-machine teaming. Finally, the findings can help emergency managers better train their volunteers who comb through social media using their understanding of the local knowledge and built environment to help machines see new patterns in data.  Hence, this project supports NSF's mission to promote the progress of science and to advance the nation's health, prosperity, and welfare by articulating the unique value that both humans and computers bring that can lead to better decisions during disasters.  The goal of this research is to better understand the real-time decisions that human annotators make under different environmental constraints, and how those contribute to the learning of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models. Under time constraints and information overload, human decision-making capabilities are limited; yet, humans still have a unique ability to understand the contextual references to the structures in the built environment that machines cannot recognize. For example, the meaning of the tweet, “Memorial is overloaded,” -- which means the hospital, called Memorial, is out of beds for patients —- can be lost on AI systems that lack the knowledge of the built environment. This example demonstrates the value that humans in the loop offer in a human-AI teaming context.  

This research focuses on capturing the ephemeral data from a variety of social media sources and our two research thrusts include: 1) online observations of Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) volunteers and a manager (a collaborator on this project) using think-aloud and cognitive interviewing strategies to reveal the real-time mental models used to make coding decisions for annotation tasks; and 2) an empirical analysis of different sampling algorithms for active (machine) learning paradigms to develop a typology of machine errors under diverse contexts that affect the quality of human decision making for annotation. This research will generate design guidelines that bridge the gap between the mechanisms used for real-time data processing with AI models and the understanding of context contributed by a human user teaming with the AI models.  Using theories of human decision-making combined with knowledge of how AI functions, this project provides a real-time, mid-disaster examination of 1) how humans understand, process, and interpret social media messages, and 2) how to refine AI algorithms to optimize active learning paradigm. This understanding will provide a theoretical framework enabling future research to develop protocols to optimize human-AI teaming by using concepts such as motivation and information theory. This work can help emergency managers conduct better training of their CERT volunteers and other annotators and provide clearer guidelines for how to communicate the unique value that humans bring to the annotation process for AI systems. Both our protocols and developed understanding of how humans interact with AI systems will be helpful for global health organizations, local and state-level disaster decision-makers, as well as provide direction for the vast CERT network in the United States.

Very little is currently known about how to leverage the skills of humans and machines when they work together (human-machine teaming) to identify meaningful patterns in social media data. Therefore, the fundamental issues this project addressed are 1) understanding the process of real-time decisions that human digital volunteers make when they rapidly convert social media data into structured codes the machine (Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms) can understand for filtering actionable information, and 2) using this knowledge to improve human-machine teaming for improving the machine processing to rapidly filter streams of social media data at scale. 


The intellectual merit of this project includes the improved understanding of the real-time decision-making that human annotators make under different environmental constraints, and how those contribute to the learning of AI models. We developed an online interview and observation protocol to collect real-time data when humans are labeling social media messages, which would be used by an AI model to automate the categorization and filtering of messages at scale. We demonstrated that active learning-based AI models can be trained, and human labelers from local communities can effectively correct the automatically-inferred erroneous labels by an AI model in a real-time disaster. We further determined that having a community partner that is committed to the project is essential for the success of this type of community-engaged research. The above findings have resulted in updating the design of a social media filtering tool (CitizenHelper, resulting from a prior-funded NSF CRII project) for a human-machine teaming approach by improving its active learning-based interface to effective solicit labeling feedback from local volunteers. 


The broader impact of this project includes a generalizable human-machine teaming approach that reveals and leverages the unique abilities that both humans and machines bring when working together, especially to comprehend social media patterns during an evolving disaster. It supported education and diversity by providing research experiences to a diverse group of seven students for interdisciplinary problem-solving, teaching teamwork, as well as developing skills for social media analytics and human-machine teaming. Finally, the findings can help emergency managers in local communities better train their volunteers who comb through social media using their understanding of the local knowledge and built environment to help machines see new patterns in data. For instance, we extensively collaborated with the Community Emergency Response Teams (CERTs) led by Montgomery County CERT in the Washington D.C. Metro region for social media filtering to find relevant information for COVID-19 pandemic response. Hence, this project supports NSF's mission to promote the progress of science and to advance the nation's health, prosperity, and welfare by articulating the unique value that both humans and computers bring that can lead to better decisions during disasters.

abstractText:
The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic is caused by a novel coronavirus, which was only identified in December 2019. Due to the novelty of the virus and the speed at which it is currently sweeping the world, not only is there very little known about the virus but there is also very little data. Despite the lack of data, there are many important questions that need to be answered. Is social distancing working effectively in `flattening the curve’? How much more effective would mandated shelter-in-place be in containing the spread? Is it worth the social cost? What is the effect of 10% of the population ignoring these protocols? What is the marginal benefit of enforcing quarantines versus implementation cost? Today the important questions seem to be related to mitigation as the biggest concern is the immediate matter at hand: the impending peak of hospitalizations due to COVID-19. However, it is also necessary to be looking ahead to a potential resurgence of this virus with a new set of questions. What will be the effect of asynchronously `opening up' different parts of the country as people are still recovering from COVID-19? How will we know we are not lifting restrictions pre-maturely? Precise answers to these questions are needed in order to make informed policy decisions, and this requires a deep understanding and accurate models of COVID-19 which are simply not available today. Unfortunately, there is no time to learn about this virus before needing to act to mitigate the tremendous damage that is already being incurred socially, economically, and even in terms of lost lives. Instead, new data must be rapidly incorporated into models and these questions must be re-visited on a constant basis to be able to quickly provide at least a reasonable understanding of the important questions above.

This project addresses the rapidly evolving modeling problem for COVID-19. Taking a systems point of view, this project seeks to investigate the effects of various overlooked artifacts of COVID-19 in the leading models used to inform policy decisions today. The numerical methods and mathematical models can provide significant complementary support to the epidemiologists worldwide on understanding how the virus spreads. The outcomes of this project will be novel stochastic and deterministic networked meta-population models as opposed to the commonly seen lumped population models. The models developed will expand simple Susceptible-Infected-Removed (SIR) models to capture a number of different properties specific to COVID-19 by adding more compartments. These models will provide a more rigorous analysis of the network effects of the ongoing pandemic which may prove especially useful as different parts of the country, or even the world, are imposing/lifting various levels of mobility restrictions at different times.

projectOutComesReport:
This project began as the COVID-19 pandemic was just unfolding. At the start of this project, there were many unknowns about the virus and the primary goal was to identify properties of the virus that are most important in properly modeling and tracking the spread of the virus through the world. In particular our research focused on two aspects overlooked in many other endeavours: the abnormally long incubation period and the effects of travel. 

The ultimate goal of this project was to develop new methods and technologies for better tracking/containing epidemics that are unfolding in real-time. The main challenge identified as a result of this project is how to synthesize data sets collected in completely different ways/places. For example, how should an individual decide exactly when to go to the grocery store, or which one, depending on the data unfolding around the individual? 

Solving this problem requires new multi-scale modeling, analysis, and control methods that is able to incorporate data collected at completely different granularities and provide individual-level recommendations to end-users. As a result of this project, it is hopefuly that new apps developed for future epidemic outbreaks can serve the public better than the various COVID-19 apps that were released in 2020-2021. e.g., many apps were able to let users know when someone they have come in contact with tested positive, but what behavioral changes should be made in response to this type of information was completely absent. Instead, future apps should combine individual-level data with regional data to make better individualized recommendations to help protect the indivudal while also better containing the epidemic on a larger scale (e.g., when to get tested, which grocery stores to avoid, when to stay home from work).

abstractText:
This Rapid Response Research (RAPID) grant will develop the Models for Assessing Strategies for Hospitals (MASH) in Pandemics (MASH-Pandemics) Portal with requisite modeling capabilities urgently needed by hospitals and regions in responding to the COVID-19 pandemic. Important perishable, time-sensitive data and information to support this effort will be collected. MASH-Pandemics will build on previously developed sophisticated, detailed discrete-event simulation-based hospital capacity and capability analysis models of typical U.S. urban hospitals. This RAPID project will support the re-specification of these models, data collection, model runs, and results analysis, outcomes from which will aid hospital administrators and regions in making optimal operational changes and collaboration plans enabled through state and national emergency declarations in response to the COVID-19 outbreak. An online portal will be constructed on which details of the modeling capabilities, practical findings and recommendations, along with potential policy implications, for responding to the COVID-19 pandemic will be posted. Additionally, run requests from hospitals, hospital collaborations and geographical regions will be taken through the portal. This work will generate crucial synthetic data needed to develop quick recommendations and analyses in a period where time is of the essence. Key outputs will include, for example: potential for various modified operational strategies to benefit hospital performance and patient survival, hospital collaboration strategies to aid regional response, anticipating critical supply needs to mobilize and prioritize support from supply chains (or Federal response capabilities), and recommendations for effective implementation of capacity enhancement strategies (alternative standards of care, modified operations, demand management). The project will provide input to educational activities in the future, once the project is complete and the pandemic subsides. The focus of this work during the period of performance will be on providing, as quickly as possible, crucially needed recommendations to hospitals and regions based on results from runs of high-quality models. 

This RAPID award will advance mathematical modeling techniques for capturing critical hospital services during crises. It employs concepts of open queuing networks, discrete event simulation, stochastic modeling, transient system analysis, and statistical methods. The work will collect critical, perishable data, and will generate crucial synthetic data for rapid analysis and prediction urgently needed in this period of a global COVID-19 pandemic. With its quantitative approach, the project will enhance hospital readiness, capacity and capability, by identifying means for efficiently using severely limited, critical personnel and physical resources, the allocation of which will affect the survival of potentially thousands of lives and the safety of health care workers along with support staff. Findings from this effort will directly support hospitals at the front line, or regions in COVID-19 “hot spots,” by providing the opportunity to request runs and receive analyses of the effectiveness of COVID-19 response strategies and collaboration mechanisms. It is anticipated that the run requests will come in a variety of forms, requiring data collection, modeling work, investigation to capture stochastic processes with input distributions and parameters, and results analyses. The models can be quickly enhanced and mobilized, and initial findings and recommendations made public in only weeks.

projectOutComesReport:
This project extended previously developed whole-hospital, resource-constrained, patient-based, stochastic, discrete-event simulation (DES) modeling capabilities to provide quantitative tools for assessing hospital capacity for serving COVID-19 pandemic patients. The models incorporate COVID-19 care paths and accompanying work flows, special equipment including ventilators and personal protective equipment, modifications to operations, including repurposing of hospital space, and the application of crisis standards of care. The models build on a generic 200-bed urban U.S. tertiary hospital serving routine emergency and COVID-19 patients. Four surge levels were considered that correspond with changing COVID-19 pandemic conditions of a hospital's service area: Getting Ready, Initial Onset, Outbreak, and Hot Spot. Systematically-designed, numerical experiments were conducted to assess potential strategies for increasing hospital capacity to handle demand surges and considers the timing for implementing and withdrawing these strategies as surge demand ebbs and flows. Numerical details of these and numerous other findings are given in five journal articles and on the team site: mash-pandemics.vse.gmu.edu. Example outcomes:

Outbreak: Implementing Crisis Standards or Other Interventions for Added Capacity

Finding 1. Treatments that reduce COVID-19 patient intensive care length of stay (LOS) by one day increase a hospital's ICU capacity by 24%.

Hot Spot: Unified COVID-19 Care Increases Capacity

Finding 2. COVID-19 designated hospitals can serve up to five times the number of COVID-19 patients compared with a similar facility accepting mixed patients.

Switch Points

Finding 3. There are two key switch points when hospitals must introduce strategies for increasing capacity or dedicate all resources to COVID-19 treatment to meet COVID-19 patient surge. Without such action, it may become necessary to ration care. A hospital can prepare for action by predicting the timing of these points.

To meet surge demand, many hospitals have needed to convert space and reassign personnel and equipment resources to the ICU and isolation rooms. The project developed additional tools to support hospital managers in taking decisions related to COVID-19 patient treatment in extreme surge conditions. To this end, a mixed-integer mathematical program with embedded equations using concepts of queueing theory and Jackson networks was developed for estimating steady-state maximum capacity in COVID-19 patient care that can be gained from repurposing space and optimally reassigning a heterogeneous staff within a hospital to create a COVID-19 only facility. An alternative closed-form, equation-based approach was created that decision-makers without optimization or software expertise can use to obtain similar estimates.

Community-based nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) have been used throughout the COVID-19 pandemic to "flatten the curve." Considering transient operational conditions, this project quantified the value of "flattening"
the curve on the risk of a hospital bed shortage even when the total number of patients in need of critical pandemic-related hospital care remains constant. It asked, "Why is a flatter curve better?"

Flattening the Curve

Finding 4. The higher the acceleration in pandemic patient demand growth, the greater the impact of the intervention. Cutting this acceleration by 75% from the greatest studied rate created over four additional weeks to prepare for an 80% risk of running out of intensive care beds.

The project also contributed to the development of methodologies for assessing the resilience of hospitals to cyberattacks and analyzing the effects of different response strategies.

Ransomware Attack

Finding 5. In the generic study hospital, paying the ransom resulted in short-term gains, but did not pay off in the longer term.

The project also developed techniques for estimating the maximum number of pandemic patients with intensive care and/or in-patient, isolation requirements that can be served by a consortium of hospitals in a region before requesting external resources. Estimates can provide an upper bound on the number of patients that can be treated within a region if all hospital resources are re-allocated for pandemic care. Methodologically, it was found that a giant, single hospital representation of all regional resources can provide a tight upper bound on the maximum hospital capacity for surge demand for a coalition.

This project sought to capture details from the field as conditions unfold. The work pivoted numerous times to capture changing pandemic dynamics, access to quickly shifting and growing expert information and changing protocols, and changing COVID-19 variant characteristics. The use of synthetic data developed from runs of a simulator eliminated issues of confounding affects from the simultaneous occurrence of regional response actions and/or changes in resources, treatments and other situational circumstances that arises from real patient data. It also provides insights without the need for internal review or the possibility of disclosing personal information.

Estimates and findings obtained through this project can aid in assessing regional healthcare capacity during surges in pandemic patient demand, predicting shortfalls, and designing preparedness and response actions. Developments from this work have been integrated within the content of an optimization course. The project benefited greatly from the cooperation of the World Bank Group and numerous individuals.

This 1-year project is to enable the participation of graduate students and early-career researchers at the Hinode-14 / IRIS-11 Joint Science Meeting, which will be held at George Mason University during July 28-31, 2020.  The meeting will highlight the most recent achievements of the Hinode and IRIS space missions together with the latest research advancements on topics related to the missions’ goals.  To date, these two satellites have provided an incredible amount of physical insights regarding the dynamics of the solar atmosphere, in particular how energy is released in the solar corona, how solar flares evolve, how eruptive events occur, and what the sources of the solar wind are.  The  present joint meeting will put special emphasis on the synergies with the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope  (DKIST), which is supported by the NSF.  Furthermore, science topics that include close cooperation and coordination with other ground-based facilities and recent space-based missions, such as the Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter, are also solicited in the invited talks as well as in the call for abstracts.  The following science themes are identified by the Scientific Organization Committee, and the relevant topics will be organized around these themes: (i) connection to inner heliosphere platforms; (ii) photospheric convection and solar magnetic field; (iii) atmospheric heating: chromosphere to corona; (iv) flares, jets, and Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs); and, (v) DKIST science and workforce development.  The research and EPO agenda of this 1-year project supports the Strategic Goals of the AGS Division in discovery, learning, diversity, and interdisciplinary research.

The goal of this project is to support the Hinode-14 / IRIS-11 Joint Science Meeting, originally planned as an in-person meeting at the Arlington Campus of George Mason University, Arlington, Virginia, USA. Due to COVID-19 pandemic, the meeting was postponed multiple times from its original planned date of July 28-31, 2020. The meeting successfully took place on October 25-29, 2021. It was hosted by George Mason University (Fairfax, VA, USA). The meeting highlighted the most recent achievements of the IRIS and Hinode missions together with the latest research on topics related to the missions? goals. The science program was organized around four themes: (1) Hinode/IRIS connection to inner heliospheric platforms (PSP, SolO and other instrumetnts), (2) photospheric convection and solar magnetic field, (3) atmospheric heating: chromosphere to corona and (4) Flares, jets, CMEs and others. The fifth day was dedicated to a tutorial to the usage of data from EIS, XRT and SOT, and SunPy and IRISpy software packages. 

There were 350 registrations from 26 countries.  There were 138 abstracts submitted, distributing in 50 oral presentations (14 invited) and 88 posters. The meeting acknowledges support from NSF, GMU, NSO, NASA and SCOSTEP/PRESTO. The full meeting information can be accessed at http://hinode14.org

abstractText:
The ability to observe the Earth from space at relevant spatial and temporal scales is key to understanding how hydrological and ecological systems will respond to climate change. In particular, high spatial and temporal resolution (meter scale, daily frequency) observations of snow-covered areas in mountain regions are critical as snow is important for water resources, driving the seasonal hydrological regimes of the Western U.S., with significant impacts on ecological communities. Planet Labs, Inc. (Planet) is a promising new source of commercial Cubesat high-resolution imagery that can be used in environmental science, as it has both high spatial (3.0-4.0 m) and temporal (1-2 day) resolution. This project will develop open-source, cloud-based cyberinfrastructure including an automated pipeline for processing, analyzing and interpreting Planet Cubesat image data using a machine learning approach to infer snow cover at meter-scale resolution. All models and data products will be openly available for use and modification by scientific communities. The project will support the training of students, postdocs and other early-career researchers through training events, special interest groups, and incubator programs. 

Currently, remotely-sensed snow observations with adequate temporal (daily) resolution are either captured at a spatial scale far too large to be relevant to high-resolution hydrology and ecology studies (e.g. MODIS, 500m) or are appropriate in spatial scale (1-10 m) but have inadequate temporal resolution and are cost-prohibitive (e.g. airborne LiDAR). The recent increase of commercial Earth Observation data with high spatiotemporal resolution may bridge the gap between ground-based and low-resolution satellite observation data. This project will focus on using convolutional neural networks-based models to couple ground and airborne-derived snow observations with Planet imagery in three different montane systems in Washington, California, and Colorado. These sites have very good coverage of ground and airborne snow observations at high resolution (3m) collected by the NASA Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) and SnowEx missions, which will be used in the training and validation of the models. The project will develop advanced cyberinfrastructure using scalable virtual machines, distributed collaborative architecture, reusable computational frameworks, and replicable machine learning workflows to empower Earth scientists to access, process and generate high-resolution snow products from Cubesat data. The project will adopt open-source strategies and ensure that all data, algorithms, and architecture comply with FAIR data principles and reproducibility and will include training materials that promote the adoption of the infrastructure and tools.

projectOutComesReport:
Mountain snowpack provides critical water for forest and meadow ecosystems experiencing rapid change due to global warming.  Accurate characterization of snow cover around trees and in forest gaps is essential for effective natural resource management in montane forest ecosystems and for advancing our understanding of the critical interactions between forests and snow processes. Snow cover mapping at meter-scale resolution is also important for monitoring meadow ecosystems. Snow impacts vegetation phenology (life stages for plant species such as flowering) and downstream hydrological systems. This project advanced snow hydrology research by pioneering the application of machine learning-based snow mapping workflows for snow identification in meter-scale spatial resolution optical imagery. By experimenting with different types of machine learning models, we've showcased the efficacy of both classical ML approaches (e.g., random forest) and deep learning for identifying snow at a 3-5 meter scale using Planetscope optical imagery from Planet. 

Within this project, we created open-source software and reproducible workflows for model reusability and broader application. We showed that machine learning models are effective when used with data from sensors with limited radiometric information, such as Planetscope imagery. Our first model used the Planetscope red, green, blue, and near-infrared information and a deep-learning segmentation model to derive snow cover maps. The model was trained using a dataset from California and then additionally tested in Colorado, a different geographic region. We then extended this model to include other features such as those derived from topographic information. Finally, we also trained a random forest model and evaluated the quality of the model-derived snow maps across various land cover types, including mountain meadows and forested areas. We found that the random forest model has a performance comparable to the more sophisticated deep-learning models while being easier to train and use. As a case study, we tested the model performance across 7,741 mountain meadows in the Sierra Nevada, California, and evaluated the model performance as a function of meadow size and shape complexity. 

Our workflows have been integrated within the advanced Geoweaver system, ensuring they are not only robust and reliable but also reusable, extendable, and adherent to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. These workflows are published as GitHub repositories under the MIT license and registered in Zenodo for citation, freely accessible for use and modification by the snow hydrology community. By harnessing Geoweaver's capabilities, our workflows are poised for broader adoption and application within the scientific community, facilitating collaborative research and accelerating advancements in snow hydrology.

In addition to technological advancements, our project has actively engaged with the scientific community through various community activities. We developed an educational Jupyter book, providing researchers and students with comprehensive resources for applying machine learning to geospatial data analysis. The content of the educational material has also been delivered in person at a hands-on training event organized at the University of Washington and online in 2023. Furthermore, we shared our experience using machine learning in an interview and blog post with  Earth Science Information Partners, ESIP,  a nonprofit organization that provides a neutral space for exciting cross-domain collaborations. These community-driven initiatives have not only facilitated knowledge exchange but have also catalyzed interdisciplinary collaboration, pushing the boundaries of snow hydrology research. 

The impact of our project extends beyond the scientific community, with broader social implications for water resource management, ecosystem conservation, and climate change adaptation. Accurate snow mapping is critical for assessing water availability, predicting flood risks, and monitoring ecosystem health, making our advancements in snow hydrology useful for informed decision-making and sustainable resource management. By promoting open science practices and advancing reproducible research methodologies, our project contributes to the larger goal of enhancing transparency, accountability, and trustworthiness in scientific research, ultimately fostering a culture of collaboration and innovation in the pursuit of addressing complex environmental challenges.

abstractText:
Secure computation allows multiple parties, each holding private data, to perform arbitrary computations on the joint data without revealing anything other than the desired output.  In the last fifteen years, secure computation has moved from being a purely theoretical area of research, to one that is being actively deployed in a variety of settings.  However, technical barriers to adoption still exist: the communication and computational costs are quite high.  At the same time, improvements in the last fifteen years have brought us quite near to the limit of what is feasible under standard definitions of security. This project investigates new techniques for improving the efficiency of secure computation beyond the known theoretical limits.

This project explores new security relaxations, and new methods of utilizing existing security relaxations, in order to help scale secure computation to larger volumes of data, and a larger number of participating parties. The investigators envision a fully decentralized data plane in which user data is accessible by service providers only at the discretion of the data owner.  Computations performed on this data would be subject to appropriate user-specified controls, and the results of the computations would reveal only what is minimally necessary to meet the goals of the data owner.  Service providers could still monetize the data, but without ever seeing it, and only with the explicit agreement of the owner. The project has outreach activities that introduce secure computation, privacy and cryptography to various communities in the DC area.

abstractText:
Much of science is found in peer-reviewed journals. However, researchers in the history or sociology of science cannot study what is accepted and what is rejected in these journals because until recently they did not have access to a body of data that included accepted and rejected manuscripts, the topics covered, the characteristics of those who submitted manuscripts, and the comments of the reviewers.  Moreover, they did not have such data over time, so that they might see changes within a discipline in terms of topics and submitters.  The American Sociological Association (ASA) has electronic copies of all the manuscripts and all the reviews for ASA journals for a twenty-year period between 1991 and 2010.  Based on a prior three-year, NSF-funded project, the Center for Social Science Research (CSSR) at the George Mason University has created a Digital Archive that contains this information for the American Sociological Review, the ASA’s top journal.   Given the complexities of the Archive data file, in June 2019 CSSR held a two-day workshop so that interested scholars could be trained to use it to answer critical questions about the history and development of sociology in a time-period of pronounced changes in the discipline.  Demand for the first Workshop was high and its documented success have prompted the need for a second workshop.  Faculty trained in the use of the archive will pass on this knowledge to their colleagues in sociology and other disciplines to further the study of the peer-review system for a flagship journal. This project is beneficial because it allows for scrutiny of the scientific process.

This project will support a two-day workshop to be held in April 2020 to train a new group of faculty and graduate students in the use of the ASA/Mason American Sociological Review (ASR) Digital Archive.  The Center for Social Science Research (CSSR) at the George Mason University has created a Digital Archive of more than 8,000 manuscripts and 26,000 reviews. The Archive includes demographic and institutional information of authors and reviews over a 20-year time-span.  The Archive was created by examining all submitted manuscripts, matching them with reviewers, and using the internet to secure other information about authors and reviewers. This information was merged into four types of files—author, reviewer, person, and manuscript files. Workshop participants will become familiar with the files and learn how to link them and/or how to use each separately, depending on the research question to be answered. Examining these files allows researchers to determine whether the peer networks of reviews are intellectually distant from those of authors, or whether both the author and the reviewer are in the same networks, thus suggesting the potential for reviewer bias.

projectOutComesReport:
The intellecual merit of the project lies in making the American Sociological Review Digital Archive (DA) materials and methods available to a wide audience, including American sociologists but also academics in other fields and outside the United States. 

The broader impact will come with a critical analyis of the peer review process that may open up academic research to a more diverse set of perspectives and participants.

This funding was provided to fund a second workshop to give members of the broader research community access to the DA. A first workshop in June of 2019 was well received by close to twenty participants. As there were a number of interested researchers who could not be accommodated, funding was requested and granted for a second workshop.

Participants were selected and logistics were arranged for the second workshop in 2020.  However, due to COVID restrictions, the workshop was postponed and then cancelled. With approval from the cognizant NSF program manager, participant support funding for the workshop was used to provide staff time to build a website with the workshop materials https://cssr.gmu.edu/research-projects/digitalarchive 

While preparing the website, we continued analysis with the DA and a peer-reviewed journal article based on the data is forthcoming in the Russell Sage Foundation Journal. 

In addition, we know of two European groups that are looking at the DA as a model for studying the peer review process in European journals and a group of political science researchers at George Mason University are preparing a proposal for NSF, "Efficiency and Bias in Peer Review: Perceived Legitimacy in Algorithmic versus Human Decision Making," which will use materials from the DA to survey academics about the efficacy of the peer review process.

abstractText:
Zoonotic diseases are diseases that exist in animals and can be transmitted to humans. Zoonoses currently account for approximately 75 percent of all emerging infections worldwide. However, the factors that trigger zoonotic disease emergence and spread remain poorly understood, in part because they involve multiple species, complex inter-species and intra-species relationships, and many interacting environmental, behavioral, social, and economic factors. Middle Eastern Respiratory Syndrome-Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) presents a case in point. MERS-CoV was first identified in human beings in 2012 and has killed 36 percent of those infected, but little is known about what has led to its emergence. For example, several human cases have been traced to contact with camels imported from Africa; studies also have detected MERS-CoV in African wildlife; and while camels are a known reservoir host for MERS-CoV, it is not known if there are additional reservoirs or intermediate hosts, or how frequently and under what conditions MERS-CoV spillover occurs. This project will investigate the natural ecology of MERS-CoV in relation to broader social, economic, and environmental changes; its potential wildlife reservoirs in close contact with camels; and the potential for spillover to humans who consume, herd, and trade camels and camel products. This work is of direct importance to national security with respect to disease threats; MERS-CoV is currently on the World Health Organization's priority shortlist of diseases in urgent need of accelerated research.  


To understand when and under what conditions MERS-CoV emerges and spreads from animals to humans, the researchers ask, (1) How do social, cultural and behavioral characteristics of camel economics shape virus ecologies? (2) Which intra- and inter-species interactions increase MERS-CoV emergence and transmission? and (3) What climatic and environmental variables are associated with transmission? Researchers will conduct field studies of wild and domestic (camel) reservoirs, collecting roughly 800 samples from targeted wildlife (ungulates and eulipotyphlads) over two years at four locations. They will carry out socio-behavioral studies across the camel value chain and follow individual camels longitudinally to determine when the same individuals seroconvert to MERS-CoV positive status. They will conduct laboratory analyses and do viral sequencing. The researchers will integrate the data into mathematical models using the 'Method of Plausible Parameter Sets' (MPPS), which will determine which mechanistic scenarios are consistent with observed patterns of MERS-CoV in camels and humans. This broadly inclusive approach expands upon traditional studies of zoonotic disease emergence. The transmission models will be applicable to other zoonotic diseases linked to livestock production and will help to identify interventions to reduce disease emergence and transmission.

projectOutComesReport:
In 2018, the team received about $2.5 million for the project entitled, "Ecology of Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) in camels, humans, and wildlife in Ethiopia."

The study investigated the natural ecology of MERS-CoV in Ethiopia in relation to broader social, economic, and climatic changes; its potential wildlife reservoirs in close contact with camels; and the potential for spillover to humans who consume, herd, and trade camels and camel products.

The ultimate goal of this study was met and it was to demonstrate that emerging disease systems, where there are insufficient data to draw statistical conclusions about risk factors for trigger events, can still be understood via causal analysis. Because the social, cultural, and economic contexts in which diseases emerge and spread are often black-boxed, only theorized in retrospect, and rarely incorporated into mathematical models, it was important to systematically collect data about each of these contexts using multi-disciplinary research methods. We collected quantitative and qualitative data about the social, cultural, and economic factors that can be triggers for disease emergence and transmission and identified several that were associated with MERS-C0V. This was the first study to integrate social, cultural, economic, biological, environmental, and climatic factors of zoonotic disease emergence and transmission on a large scale and created a blueprint that can be used to continue to study MERS-CoV and other emerging zoonotic diseases.

We developed and applied the Method of Plausible Parameter Sets, an innovative new approach developed in the study team’s lab to determine which mechanistic climate-animal-human scenarios are consistent with observed patterns of MERS-CoV emergence and transmission and are plausible.  Our preliminary results uncovered that MERS-CoV emergence is dependent on season as it was only identified in less than 10% of samples and only during 1 season.  Humans who had no direct contact with camels had active infection while camels who had a history of movement had evidence of previous MERS-CoV infection.

The models generated to understand MERS-CoV in African camel economies may also be applied to investigate other viral zoonotic diseases that are linked to camel economies. Camel economies are complex because they include both traditional and emergent practices. The study presents methods to study both and our results show how these two types of practices come together. The project led to several multi-disciplinary training opportunities for graduate and undergraduates from the fields of anthropology, biology, epidemiology, geography, and mathematics. This project was presented as a case study in 4 courses (1 to undergraduates and 3 to graduate students) reaching over 60 students. Two undergraduates, 6 graduate students, and 2 post-doctoral scientistis analyzed data that emerged from this study as part of research assistantships, thesis projects and indepnent studies. The protocols and case studies will be made publicly available as teaching modules on the use of anthropological and ecological theories for zoonotic disease research for use in medical, public health, veterinary, biology, and mathematics curricula. Maps of African camel economies have been developed for use in publications stemming from this project and highlight how changes in temperature and precipitation, food availability, and resources for camel production impact camel movement and their interaction with humans and wildlife. Results were disseminated to local communities in meetings with ministry officials and other interested parties in Ethiopia and elsewhere.
